title: Xuanning (Alex) Zhang
text:
Hello, I’m Alex, a Master of Business Analytics student at Monash University with a background in Banking and Finance. I’m interested in how data can help us understand financial markets and make better decisions.
During my undergraduate studies, I learned how financial markets work and what can cause them to become unstable. My projects included building a simulated investment portfolio for an investor concerned about risk and responsible investing, studying the Société Générale trading scandal, and exploring how Japan’s low interest rates influenced currency trading. I also studied project management, organisational behaviour and business ethics.
In my master’s degree, I’ve been learning how to turn data into clear and useful findings. I used government statistics to explore changes in Australia’s seafood industry and worked with a team to compare renewable energy use and carbon emissions across four countries. I’ve also examined how mistakes when combining datasets can affect the results of an analysis. I use R and the tidyverse to analyse data, Quarto to present my work, and Git to track changes and collaborate.
I aim to make my work clear, honest and easy to check. This means explaining my methods, documenting my steps, sharing code where appropriate and taking care with data privacy. Through this blog, I’m practising how to explain data and research to people without a technical background.
I’m particularly interested in bringing together finance and data analysis. I’m always happy to connect with others interested in financial markets, data analysis or visualisation.

title: Did climate change make Black Summer fires more likely in Australia?
text: The sky turned orange over southeastern Australia in the summer of 2019-20. The “Black Summer” bushfires burned more than 19 million hectares of land, killed 34 people and destroyed around 5900 homes and other buildings. Smoke blanketed cities like Sydney and Canberra, there were nearly 80% Aussies said they were affected. Perhaps you were one of them. So, is it only a disaster season or did human-caused climate change played a role? A major international research found that comparing with around 1900, human-caused climate change has made the occurrence of dangerous fire weather at least 30% more likely, and possibly much more (Oldenborgh et al. 2021).

title: Did climate change make Black Summer fires more likely in Australia?
section: What happened? And what did scientists asked?
text:
What happened? And what did scientists asked?
In that summer, many people watching this news asked this question, but it is harder to answer than it sounds. A bushfire need ingredients of hot weather, strong winds, dry vegetation and source of ignition like lightning or people. Climate change will not light fires,and there has not fire season can be blamed on single one factor. So scientists asked another question: how much more the climate change increased the probability of hot, dry and windy weather that let the fire spread so far? You can even imagine that every road could happening car accident, but wet road will strongly increase the probability.
To find out, a team of international scientists has compared the likelihood of weather in “Black Summer” from 2019-20 to that around 1900. They used two kinds of evidence: the Australian weather records from 1910 and computer models of the climate, which can simulate the weather condition overtime. This evidences let scientists count out the frequency of extreme weather in different periods. The team has divided the research into three aspects: drought, extreme heat and overall fire weather.

title: Did climate change make Black Summer fires more likely in Australia?
text:
What evidence shows
The climate records for fire weather came from ERA5, which combines the previous climate observations with climate model since 1979. Scientists used the Fire Weather Index (FWI) to measure how dangerous the weather was, it can be seen as a danger score which combines the temperature, humidity, wind and rainfall into one value, higher FWI will let bushfire easier to start and spread. The research focused on the most dangerous week of each fire season, as there has more land burned in southeastern Australia with higher FWI, thus it is a useful measurement index.
These three factors reflect different situations (Table 1). Extreme heat shows a clear relationship, that human-caused climate change has let hot week in December 2019 at least twice likely. The climate record shows if the similar extreme heat happen around 1900, its temperature will be 1 to 2 °C cooler. Drought is different because the team did not find a clear relationship in human-caused extreme rainfall shortage, but it does not mean there has no effect on drought by climate change, but did not detect one. The drought in 2019 was mainly drove by two climate modes: the Indian Ocean Dipole and the Southern Annular Mode, both of them explained roughly one-third of the rain fall deficit from July to December in 2019. While all factors are considered in FWI, the result is obvious: extreme weather like “Black Summer” have at least 30% higher than around 1900 which mainly due to rise in extreme heat.




Table 1: How climate change affected three factors in Black Summer’s weather comparing to around 1900











Factor
Findings
Explanation




Extreme heat
At least twice as likely
Heat wave in 2019 Dec will been 1-2 °C cooler if it happen in around 1900


Extreme rainfall shortages
No human-caused trend found
Can’t reject it, the research did not detect a trend in the drought


Extreme fire weather
At least 30% more likely
Mainly because extreme heat became more likely








According to ERA5 climate records, the probability of fire weather like “Black Summer” is at least four times higher than around 1900 (Figure 1). The model also suggest that in a world 2°C warmer than pre-industrial level, the disaster climate will be at least four times than the beginning of 20th century. Also, the risk has already risen and predicted to keep rising.








Figure 1: The extreme fire weather as Black Summer is now more likely than around 1900. Plot shows the minimum increase reported by research.





These data come with an important limitation, the climate model tend to underestimate how quickly extreme heat has increased, thus the actual increased risk could be larger than expectation. Furthermore, the climate data only cover the time after 1979, but there was a drying trend in this period and may make the “four times” too high, the 2°C projection is also based on two models. That is why we should focus on cautious lower bounds rather than the most dramatic numbers.

title: Did climate change make Black Summer fires more likely in Australia?
text:
Not just a bad summer
Back to our question: Did climate change caused Black Summer? Climate change did not light the fires. The evidence shows human-caused climate change increased the probability of dangerous fire weather mainly because it make extreme heat more frequent. The likelihood of extreme heat week in December 2019 has increase at least twice as likely as that around 1900 and fire weather like 2019-20 has increased at least 30%, and this risk is still increasing. The research did not find a clear trend of human-caused rain fall deficits and drought is still an open question.
What does this mean for you? If you living in southeastern Australia, the fire weather like Black Summer is not as rare as a century ago, but more common due to global warming. Here are few simple steps: Check the danger rating on hot days, cleaning dry leaves and plants near your house on time and set a bushfire plan. No one can stop every fire, but better understanding of risk can help us be ready for the next Black Summer.
